Hub·Now, next and how to help

Where Horizonis going.

What is being done, what comes next, what shipped and where you can help. No dates: things are Now, Next or Later. Read it in plain words, or switch to the technical picture.

Horizon is Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3 rewritten from scratch in Rust, so it runs faster on the same computer. Single player, LAN, servers, resource packs and Horizon's own mods work today, on your own copy of the game.A native Rust and wgpu reimplementation of Java 26.3: the same saves, rules and terrain, checked against the real game by more than 300 differential harnesses (a Java oracle and a Rust probe on the same inputs). Single player runs on its own server thread, like vanilla's integrated server.

Being done now

  1. 01Steady frames at long render distancesMaking Horizon faster than vanilla on every computer, with smooth camera movement even at 32 chunks, by spreading the work better over the processor's cores.Frame pacing at render distance 32 (#678): long frames come from work competing with the render thread. In review: no main-thread tick stutter at high render distances (#3827), each proto chunk's light view built once (#3815), video memory handed back by the vertex arena (#3466), chunk batches assembled on helper threads (#3036), free structure starts in the generation workers (#1760). Still open: far terrain at 48 to 64 chunks (#718) and CPU-bound fields of block entities (#717). Every change shows before and after numbers from tools/perf_bench.py against vanilla 26.3 (docs/benchmark.md).
  2. 02Modpacks' world generation, nativelyMaking the world-generation mods of popular modpacks (new structures, YUNG's dungeons and mineshafts, packs built on Lithostitched) generate their worlds in Horizon, natively and fast.horizon-port-pack carries a pack's data-driven content over, and 26.2 data packs are upgraded to 26.3's format (#3369). In review: worlds taller than 32 sections and each level's shape from its dimension type (#3480, #3488), data-pack biomes in local and remote worlds (#3491), block state providers (#3802), surface rules by biome id (#3366), Lithostitched's pool and processor modifiers (#1777). Mods whose Java code does more than world generation don't run (docs/modpacks.md).
  3. 03Single player as a server: the last differencesSingle player now runs a small server in the background, as vanilla does. We are fixing what still behaves differently there; every fix also works for LAN and server players.Since #1514 single player runs on the server thread (game/integrated.rs) and the window joins it as a client. The open [server-thread] issues list the gaps. In review: breeding's advancement and statistic (#3873), the client's menu when the server replaces the player (#3841), splashes when falling in water (#3621). docs/server-levels.md.
  4. 04Vanilla parity: the player-visible gaps, closedEvery method of the Java game is tracked with where Horizon does it, and the differences players can see are being closed, list by list: mobs, blocks, items, screens, rendering, servers.The port ledger (tools/port_ledger.py, tools/port_map/, #3139) gives every 26.3 method a verdict and links the harnesses that cover it (#3526). The player-visible gaps are ten lists, one per area (#3512 to #3521); a fix translates the vanilla method, ticks its row and carries the parity label. Start from .claude/skills/vanilla-parity.
  5. 05ModsMods for Horizon, as one line of work led by the modding team: native mods the launcher builds into your game, mods on servers, mod screens and settings, tools for mod makers, the registry and machines.One item for all modding work (#3911), led by levzzz5154 with vladislav_hagen; the order between the parts is theirs. Native mods on stable hook points (game/native_hooks.rs, #3345, #3346, #3434, #3435) built by the launcher (#3388, #3855); server-side hooks (#3878, #3706); mod-owned screens, input and drawing; tools for mod makers (templates, native.py check); the registry (#1634, #1642, #1659); machines with inventories and menus (#1189); mods that read and change the world through the server. docs/native-mods.md.

  7. 07One single-player path: remove the in-frame worldSingle player has one way to run, the server thread, so every fix works everywhere and there are fewer bugs. See also 'Single player as a server' and docs/server-levels.md.Gameplay parity
  8. 08Faster block lookupsSpeeding up the code that reads and writes the blocks of the world, which almost everything in the game goes through: generation, lighting, meshing and ticking.PalettedContainer and PackedStorage find an entry's word by multiply and shift instead of an integer division (#1790, #1794); meshing looks up baked models by index, not by name (#1747). Each change keeps the paletted storage harnesses identical and shows its microbenchmark (docs/performance/paletted-container-access-results.md).Performance
  9. 09Playing on servers: everything shows as it shouldWhen you play on a server, other players, mobs, items and menus look and behave as in vanilla: skins, poses, item names, inventories and server networks.Client-of-a-server fixes in game/remote*.rs and horizon-protocol: mobs' aggressive and item-use flags (#1802, #1798), ghost items after a remote menu (#1795), skins (#1652), cookies and transfer packets for proxy networks (#1650), firework boosts (#1671), living-entity attributes and simulation distance (#1731), styled item names (#1702), primed TNT between updates (#1710).Servers and multiplayer
  10. 10Shader packs, written again from scratchShader packs were removed and are being rebuilt from scratch. They come back, off by default, once the best-known packs draw properly.A clean-room rewrite in horizon-shaderpack, from the packs' public format documentation only: reading packs, the preprocessor and .properties files are merged (#1584, #1585, #1586); translating programs to WGSL through naga, buffers, uniforms and the terrain, entity, sky, weather and hand stages are in review (#1698 to #1801).Rendering
  11. 11A new launcher designA redesigned launcher: every button where you expect it, the fewest clicks to play, add an instance or add mods, smooth animations, and instant startup.Based on the site concept by the Team (Bricolage Grotesque, a night sky and an animated pixel sunset). Screens and flows are designed first, then small PRs; tokens in crates/horizon-theme and rules in docs/design-system.md, the game's vanilla look unchanged. Measured before and after: startup, frame time and idle CPU/GPU, reduced motion honoured. Mods screens separate Horizon native mods from Java mods; a running instance can be stopped from the launcher.Launcher
  12. 12SplitscreenPlay with a friend on the same screen, each with a controller.Issue #2054, built by martipops as a series: up to 16 local players on the server thread's multiplayer (#3541), each controller driving its own player (#3794), joining with a controller (#3801), players in windows of their own (#3825) and the profile page (#3826).Gameplay parity

How to help

Play it and tell us what differs from vanilla (Discord or GitHub), run the benchmark on your computer, vote for what you want next, or pick one of the Help wanted items.Read CONTRIBUTING.md, pick a Help wanted item or a To do card, check vanilla's code for the behaviour, and paste the block python3 tools/pr_ready.py prints in your pull request.

PerformanceOngoing

Servers that hold 20 TPS with 50 to 100 players

Servers that keep 20 ticks per second with 50 to 100 players. Today Horizon holds it up to 50 bots and drops to about 10 at 100.Measured against vanilla on equal work (docs/server.md, Scale): Horizon is ahead with few players and when exploring, but vanilla's tick is shorter with 25 to 50 players near spawn. Ideas on the list: send entity changes instead of rebuilding every entity each tick (about 15 percent), fewer memory reads in random ticks and collision scans, cheaper item collision checks, mob AI and natural spawning. The bot benchmark (horizon-bots) is the proof.

Performance

Exact far terrain from real chunks

Far terrain drawn from the world you really built and explored, caves and builds included, not only a preview from the seed.Keep a 3D mip store on disk built from real chunks, drawn by the GPU beside the seed preview for areas nobody has visited. Written from scratch and measured before it is kept. Builds on Far Detail and the far-terrain levels of detail already shipped; the open work on them is #718.

#718

Performance

A batch of targeted optimisations

Several smaller speed-ups, each measured: idle block entities that sleep, cheaper particles, faster structure placement, high-rate mice and very large texture packs.Block entities and hoppers that skip work when idle (the hopper item scan is already skipped when no item is near); a particle frustum test first (also a parity gap), then particle quads built on the GPU; jigsaw shortcuts that skip blocked connectors and pool elements known not to fit, with layouts unchanged (trial chambers and ancient cities first); batched raw mouse input on Windows for 8000 Hz mice; a better atlas packer for huge resource packs (a 64x pack builds a 704 MiB atlas for 452 MiB of textures); sign-heavy scenes (#1461). Profile first, keep what pays, show before and after numbers.

#1461docs/profiling.md

Modpacks

Older Fabric and Forge mods

Recognise mods built for versions before 26.1 in the mod browser, so they can be checked and carried over like newer ones.A mapping table from intermediary and SRG names so pre-26.1 jars can be classified, and a rename for mod ids with dashes (fabric-api); the port step then treats them like newer jars (docs/mod-browser.md).

docs/mod-browser.md

Modpacks

A modpack's own resource and shader packs

Imported modpacks carry their resource packs into a profile of their own. Shader-pack conversion is still pending.Resource-pack carry-over is implemented locally: Modrinth common/client overrides, CurseForge's override folder, installed instances (ZIP and directory packs), and hash-checked indexed ZIP downloads. The launcher keeps profile edits and lets resource-only profiles play; packs are enabled in Resource Packs. Synthetic import and profile tests cover the file pipeline; in-game rendering has not been verified. Shader-pack conversion is still pending, so this combined item remains partial (docs/modpacks.md).

docs/modpacks.md

Modpacks

Whole modpacks, such as ATM10, rewritten

Rewriting a complete big modpack for Horizon so it runs far better than the original. Not a priority now: the work above comes first.The project's first goal for modpacks: support them ten times better than vanilla and port any of them. It was set aside in favour of compatibility through the browser. What exists: ATM10's world generates and 42 of its 496 mods are carried at least in part (docs/modpacks.md). It depends on 'Mods with code' and the native mod API.

docs/modpacks.md

Modpacks

Running Java mods that aren't rewritten

Run Java mods that nobody has rewritten for Horizon yet, through a bridge or a converter. Hard and not started: the Convert button and native rewrites come first.Earlier research (#527, closed) found that Java mods can't simply run, because they call Minecraft's own classes. Option to look at again: a bridge for simple Fabric mods.

A Convert to Rust button for what isn't rewritten yet

When a mod, shader pack or modpack hasn't been rewritten for Horizon, one button converts what can be converted, so you don't have to wait for the rewrite.Generalise the mod browser's Port step (horizon-port-pack: the data, assets, worldgen and block and item definitions of Java mods, .mrpack and CurseForge zips) to every kind of content: code mods as native mods (see 'Mods with code') and shader packs, converting an Iris/OptiFine pack into Horizon's format. The browser says what works before the install. Java code itself does not run (docs/modpacks.md, docs/mod-browser.md).

Modpacks

Mods with code: machines, magic, mobs

Making mods that add machines, magic and mobs work in Horizon, in steps, starting with machines. They are most of what a big modpack is made of.333 of the 496 mods in a big pack (ATM10) contain code. Issue #1854 ranks the gaps (ticking block entities, networking, rendering, menus, inventories) that unlock them in tiers, with machines first as the recommended path. Code mods are native mods now (docs/native-mods.md): each port is a horizon-mixins bundle. The path isn't started yet (docs/modpacks.md).

Gameplay parity

Every Minecraft version, prepared automatically

Every past and future Minecraft version prepared for Horizon automatically. When Mojang releases one, Horizon follows it, and every system is checked against it again.The port pipeline (docs/version-ports.md, tools/version_port.py) detects a release, prepares it, diffs its classes against the pinned 26.3, regenerates the data-driven tables, runs every parity harness on it and writes a port report that becomes issues. The goal is as little human work as possible for any version, past or future. Detection and the first slices are merged; the scheduled agent that runs it every day isn't installed yet. Two versions in one build are out of scope.

An optional AI teammate

Code and tools

Pipeline protection and a GitHub App for agents

Safer releases: changes to the release machinery need the owner's review, and AI agents use a smaller identity of their own instead of a personal account..github/CODEOWNERS lists the workflows, the release and signing tools, the update-checking code and the installers (#1015); the branch protection that makes it count waits for the horizon-agent GitHub App, which reads and writes code, pull requests and issues but can't change settings, workflows, secrets or members, and whose tokens last an hour. It needs the owner to create the App and switch the protection on (docs/security.md).

docs/security.md

Code and tools

Signed updates everywhere, installers included

Every download Horizon makes is checked against the project's signature, including the first install with install.sh and install.ps1.Releases carry signed checksums, and the launcher and horizon-server update refuse anything unsigned (#1011, #1014). Left: the first install through install.sh and install.ps1 still trusts only the checksum GitHub publishes, because verifying Ed25519 signatures needs OpenSSL 3, which macOS doesn't ship (docs/security.md).

Good first tasks

Each one is a small difference from vanilla, with an issue that says how to see it. Found one you like? Copy its /claim command and send it on Discord, so nobody starts the same work.

Each links its issue; the technical text says where in the code and in vanilla to start. /claim on Discord marks it as yours, /unclaim frees it.

  1. 01Benchmark your computerRun Horizon's built-in benchmark and share the report: every new computer makes the performance work more accurate. No coding needed.horizon-launcher play --arg=--benchmark --arg=standard writes a JSON report; horizon-launcher data benchmark <report> shows what would be sent and uploads it (client.crewnetwork.space/docs/performance). Results from three installs with the same hardware appear on the Benchmarks page. Example: #1711.
  2. 02End city banners keep their patternBanners in End cities show as plain magenta instead of with their pattern.Compare the banner block entities the End city templates place with vanilla's (EndCityPieces, the templates' block entity NBT, BannerBlockEntity's patterns), in crates/horizon-world/src/worldgen/structure/. Issue #1438; possibly related: #526.#1438
  3. 03Enchanted loot in End citiesArmour and tools in End city chests should come enchanted, as in vanilla.loot.rs implements enchant_with_levels: find why the End city chest table's rolls come out bare, and compare them with vanilla's for a few seeds. Issues #1437, #1660.#1437

Ways to help

Tell us what differs

Something that doesn't play like vanilla is a bug. Say what you did, what happened and what vanilla does, with your Horizon version and system.

Report a bugSuggest something(opens in a new tab)

Take a task

Pick a good first task or an open issue. On Discord, /claim 1234 tells everyone you are on issue 1234, so nobody starts the same work; /unclaim frees it.

Open issues(opens in a new tab)

Bring your AI agent

On Discord, /agent connect gives your coding agent a personal token for Kira's MCP server: it reads the work board, claims tasks and posts its progress in your name.

Join the Discord(opens in a new tab)

Benchmark your computer

Run the built-in benchmark and share the report: every new machine makes the performance work more accurate. No coding needed.

How to

Report a bug

One bug per report: something that breaks, or doesn't play like vanilla. Fill this in and it opens as a ready issue on GitHub for you to check and send, with the steps in the order the maintainers need them.

Search the open bugs first

Issues are public, so leave out passwords and personal details. A screenshot or your log file helps: add it once the issue is open (where the log is). No GitHub account? Copy it for Discord and post it in #horizon-bugs, where Kira turns it into an issue.

The rules

  1. Vanilla is the specification. Wherever Minecraft 26.3 has the feature, Horizon does exactly what it does: read vanilla's code, then match it.
  2. Small pull requests, proven. One change each, under about 500 lines, with the block python3 tools/pr_ready.py prints: formatting, Clippy, tests and the harnesses your change can affect.
  3. Say who wrote it. If an AI agent wrote or posts it, the pull request says so, and commits keep its co-author line.
  4. Never commit Mojang's files. No game jars, assets, decompiled code or prepared resources, and nothing taken from other mods' code.

CREW Client

Resmi bir Minecraft ürünü değildir. Mojang veya Microsoft tarafından onaylanmamıştır veya bunlarla ilişkili değildir.

Geliştirici & Ekip

Horizon is made by Ludovic Marie; reach him through lu4ovic.com (opens in a new tab). This site is developed by Anthony S of DezerX (opens in a new tab), who is responsible for it. Horizon contains no Minecraft code, assets or data, and this site offers no game files: you need your own legally obtained copy of Minecraft: Java Edition. Minecraft is a trademark of Mojang Synergies AB.

Lisanslar

Horizon's original work is under the MIT licence (opens in a new tab). The fonts are Geist and Geist Mono, under the SIL Open Font License (opens in a new tab). Every asset on this site is listed in LEGAL.md.

Gizlilik

This site sets no cookies, has no analytics or trackers and loads nothing from third parties except GitHub. When you open a release, the server keeps a one-way hash of your IP address so that release counts each visitor once; the address itself is never stored. To show the latest releases, patch notes, links and contributors, your browser asks api.github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com for them, and avatars.githubusercontent.com for the contributors' pictures; GitHub's privacy statement (opens in a new tab) covers those requests. The launcher sends nothing unless you allow it: what it can send, and how to delete it (opens in a new tab).
